transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-22 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Location: Zoom
Agenda: run through observed SLA gaps, agree mitigation levers, define oncall playbook + simulation plan
Attendees: Avery Chen, Marcus Li, Priya Kapoor (Redwood) — Darla Mendoza, Tomás Rivera, Hari Narayanan, Lena Park (Hudson)

Summary:
- Hudson has a recurring latency tail at 99.9p under burst traffic; customers hit perceived rate limits and some downstream retries cascade.
- Goal: define immediate mitigations (throttling, circuit breaker thresholds, fallback model routing) and produce a concise oncall playbook to triage and restore within 15m for severe incidents.
- Plan: Redwood to send runbook + perf artifacts; Hudson to provide incident timeline; schedule tabletop next week.

Topics covered:
- observed SLA gap and likely causes (batching/breakers/cache miss patterns)
- runbook entries (who pages, when to escalate, fallback to smaller quantized model)
- verification plan (benchmarks, smoke tests)
- compliance/recording concerns for postmortem

Action items (captured in metadata)

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: okay uh hey everyone thanks for joining on short notice, we'll run about an hour plus — start with the gap you saw, Darla, and then we'll walk into mitigations and the playbook, ok?
[00:14] Darla Mendoza: yeah thanks, so to summarize, over the last three spikes we saw tail latency at the 99.9 go up to 5-ish seconds for completion tokens, that translates into upstream timeouts and churn, we also had some retries from our payment gateway hitting duplicate requests.
[00:30] Tomás Rivera: and for context those spikes are usually around our batch settlement window, like 02:00 UTC, there's lots of small requests with varying seq lengths, so the KV cache hit rate drops.
[00:46] Marcus Li: okay KV cache hit rate — we saw similar in lab when sequence length variance is high the prefix cache is less effective, that increases per token compute. One quick mitigation is to pin a smaller context window for that route or use a cached prefix snapshot.
[01:05] Lena Park: just to flag compliance, any cached data in runtime needs to comply with our retention policy — we can't keep PII in cache beyond the window, so KMS/HSM integration and rotation is important.
[01:22] Avery Chen: agree, we should call out KMS keys for ephemeral cache snapshots; Redwood's Private deploys can integrate customer KMS but for hosted we'll propose a short retention TTL.
[01:37] Hari Narayanan: from an SLA perspective we need a hard SLO of 95% under 500ms average for rea-time auth checks, when that breaks we need a deterministic fallback so the system doesn't block payments.
[01:56] Marcus Li: deterministic fallback — two layers: 1) route to quantized smaller model (faster, cheaper) with lower accuracy; 2) short-circuit to cached deterministic responses for known patterns. We can put a circuit-breaker that opens at a per-route error/latency budget.
[02:20] Tomás Rivera: question — how do we avoid noisy neighbor problems when we burst? If Redwood autoscaler takes time, we need an immediate local mitigation.
[02:33] Avery Chen: right — immediate mitigations are throttle by user tier, degrade to smaller model, and enable a lite-mode which bypasses some non-critical processing. We'll document the sequence in playbook.
[02:48] Darla Mendoza: can we show the exact decision tree for oncall? who pages whom first for a severity-1?
[02:56] Priya Kapoor: yes, Eisenhower-style triage. Proposal: S1 pages SRE on-call (Hudson), Redwood on-call (SE) gets copied, if not ack within 5m escalate to engineering lead and product. We'll include runbook steps like collect timeline, check KV cache hit rate, check autoscaler events, check GPU OOMs, gather last 5 minutes of traces.
[03:24] Avery Chen: note that some of those logs require elevated access in Private; we'll include role-based links.
[03:33] Tomás Rivera: we had an incident where the autoscaler queued jobs and the runtime started returning broken streams — was that the kernel fallback you mentioned in the past?
[03:45] Marcus Li: yes, that's the kernel fallback path when a particular kernel OOMs we swap to a slower generic kernel, but in past runs that increased latencies dramatically. So we should prefer model routing over kernel fallback if low-latency is the priority.
[04:05] Darla Mendoza: can Redwood guarantee model routing won't change output semantics for critical auth checks? We can't have materially different decisions that affect fraud detection.
[04:18] Avery Chen: good point — we'll mark which routes are safe to degrade. For auth, we'll recommend a deterministic fallback only (cached decision or rule-based). For non-critical flows we can route to quantized models.
[04:34] Hari Narayanan: compliance will want to see the regression tests and evaluation prompts that validate degraded model behaviour.
[04:44] Priya Kapoor: we'll attach a short eval suite — PRs show token-level and decision-level metrics. Marcus, can we produce a small regression matrix?
[04:53] Marcus Li: yes, I'll run a targeted eval across three prompts sets: auth, settlement, and customer-notify; include accuracy delta and latency delta.
[05:05] Speaker X: [overlap] can we also include an audit trail section for the postmortem so we can satisfy internal and external auditors?
[05:12] Lena Park: exactly, auditors will want the timeline, who made config changes, and KMS access logs around the time.
[05:20] Avery Chen: we'll include a template for the postmortem that captures that.
[05:27] Tomás Rivera: ok on the concrete mitigations — what's the rollout plan and how fast can Redwood implement throttling per route?
[05:35] Marcus Li: per-route throttling is fast — we can push a rate-limit change within an hour for hosted routes. For Dedicated/Private it's a config change that Hudson/SRE can control but Redwood can ship a remote knob if you give access.
[05:51] Darla Mendoza: is there an automated fallback we can rely on without manual intervention?
[05:58] Marcus Li: yes — we can configure a policy: if 99.9p latency breaches X ms for Y consecutive minutes, flip to fallback model and reduce batch sizes. That is reversible automatically once metrics come back.
[06:16] Priya Kapoor: capture that in the playbook with exact metric names and dashboards to look at — e.g., token-latency-99p, kv-cache-hit-rate, active-gpu-allocs.
[06:31] Hari Narayanan: we also want proactive alerts when a single customer is responsible for >30% of requests at peak to avoid single-tenant saturation.
[06:42] Avery Chen: fair — we can add tenant-throttling knobs and provide recommended thresholds.
[06:49] Tomás Rivera: on logging — how heavy is span collection? We worry that tracing itself adds pressure.
[06:56] Marcus Li: tracing overhead can be tuned, sample rates for distributed traces can be dropped in heavy load and we can fall back to lightweight metrics-only until the system is stable. We'll document exact sample rates.
[07:10] Darla Mendoza: what's in the 15-minute restore playbook step-by-step?
[07:16] Avery Chen: Step 1: identify severity and page stakeholders. Step 2: apply per-route throttle and set model-route fallback. Step 3: reduce batch sizes and disable non-critical plugins. Step 4: if still degraded, redirect traffic to dedicated capacity or cancel non-essential work. Step 5: after stable, run smoke tests and resume normal policies.
[07:38] Priya Kapoor: and include rollback thresholds — e.g., once token latency P99 drops below target for 5 mins, start gradual rollforward.
[07:48] Tomás Rivera: what about capacity pre-warming for settlement windows? Can Redwood help with pre-scaled warm nodes?
[07:56] Marcus Li: yes, we can schedule warm-up capacity and pin model weights to memory before window starts — scriptable via the deployment API. We can share a terraform snippet.
[08:12] Avery Chen: I'll attach a snippet to the runbook.
[08:18] Darla Mendoza: are there any parts of Redwood's telemetry that Hudson won't see due to privacy?
[08:24] Avery Chen: in hosted mode some infra-level traces are redwood-owned but we can provide aggregated telemetry and role-based dashboards; in Private we can give full access.
[08:35] Hari Narayanan: okay compliance note — if we use hosted fallback for auth, retention of logs must be configurable because of PCI.
[08:43] Lena Park: and KMS proofs for key rotation must be provided if ephemeral cache holds any payment tokens.
[08:50] Marcus Li: we'll include a KMS rotation cadence and show how to bind secrets to VPC endpoints.
[08:59] Priya Kapoor: switch to verification plan — Marcus please describe the perf runs you'll do.
[09:05] Marcus Li: plan: 1k qps steady-state with sequence length distribution matching your peak window, plus 2-minute spike tests and 1-minute microbursts. We'll capture KV hit rate and quantized-model end-to-end latencies.
[09:20] Tomás Rivera: do we have scripts to replay live traffic anonymized?
[09:24] Marcus Li: yes we can take a sanitized sample and replay it in staging; we'll need Hudson to approve sampling and PII redaction.
[09:34] Darla Mendoza: results need to show how graceful degradation affects decision accuracy — not just token latency.
[09:41] Marcus Li: agreed — regression matrices will include decision-level metrics.
[09:47] Avery Chen: can we talk about paging and runbook ownership — who is the primary responder?
[09:52] Tomás Rivera: Hudson SRE is primary; Redwood SE becomes secondary/assist and can take ownership of debugging model/runtime issues.
[09:59] Priya Kapoor: we should list contact handoff steps: runbook link, mandatory logs to collect, and a pre-populated slack channel for incidents.
[10:10] Darla Mendoza: one more operational ask: we want nightly smoke that hits the auth route to detect regressions before morning settlement.
[10:18] Marcus Li: we can set up a synthetic job that runs and alerts on regressions — we'll provide thresholds.
[10:24] Avery Chen: ok moving to simulation plan — recommend a 60m tabletop with two scenarios: crashloop + 3x spike during window. We'll walk through runbook and time-to-restore expectations.
[10:38] Hari Narayanan: make the script include a faux config change so we test runbook friction.
[10:44] Priya Kapoor: good idea, adds real human workflow validation.
[10:48] Speaker X: quick note — link to security pack mentioned in kickoff email is not accessible to external users; can Redwood re-share?
[10:55] Avery Chen: yes I'll re-share the security pack and include the SOC2 artifacts; also include an exported list of audit log fields.
[11:05] Tomás Rivera: ok last question — is there a recommended degradation window for critical flows (how long to hold fallback before manual review)?
[11:12] Marcus Li: recommended automatic fallback for up to 30 minutes with auto-retest; if it persists beyond that escalate to SRE lead for manual intervention.
[11:22] Darla Mendoza: would be nice to have a visual decision tree PDF for the ops team.
[11:26] Avery Chen: we'll produce a short PDF and the runbook link.
[11:31] Priya Kapoor: I'll coordinate invites for the tabletop next week and make sure compliance is on the invite.
[11:36] Avery Chen: brilliant — let's recap next steps: Redwood will send runbook draft + terraform snippet + perf plan; Hudson sends incident timeline + approves anonymized replay; we schedule tabletop.
[11:48] Tomás Rivera: thanks everyone.
[11:52] Meeting closed.
